1.pericope_label: Thou hast a name that thou livest, and art dead

schools.summary: Describe the city before the church. Sart is now a mere village of paltry huts, once the capital of the old Lydian monarchy and associated with Croesus, Cyrus and Alexander, the great entrepot of dyed woollen fabrics where the art of dyeing is said to have been invented and gold-dust was found in the sand of the Pactolus, laid waste by an earthquake under Tiberius and given over to a worship of Cybele whose rites encouraged impurity; the judgments that have stuck to it are the city of Death and a contrast of past splendour and present unresting decline. On the titles, notice a change from the opening vision: there he was seen holding the stars in his right hand, here he is said to have the seven Spirits and also the stars, and it is hard to overlook the unhesitating way in which he is spoken of as owning the Spirit who alone can make the angels of his Church shine; the stars mean also that he has entire control over the ministers of the churches and could remove them at pleasure. On the deadness, notice what the other letters make conspicuous by its absence, that no prevailing error or false doctrine is specified here as at Ephesus and Thyatira, so that the complaint is a simple want of religion. Then diagnose the mechanism: living with the credit of superior piety, it was easy to grow satisfied with the reputation, and self-satisfaction is the road to self-deception. On the remedy, render the command become wakeful, for it will not do to rouse and sleepily grasp at one's weapons, or even to stand for once at arms; and observe that Christ does not say arise from the dead, since there are vestiges of life.

Hear the call to remember as addressed to your own age, taking Sardis for the church since the Reformation and the things received and heard for the doctrines of grace preached by Luther and others, now almost buried in forgetfulness — this is exactly our case. Alongside that, give the ecclesiastical history of the place, the pastors and bishops of Sardis century by century.

Make the deadness a matter of withdrawal, that the Spirit, having been repeatedly grieved, is about finally to depart; they have the reputation of Christians and consequently of being alive to God, but have not the life of God in their souls. Say the same of the doers as others say of the works, that they performed duties of all kinds but no duty completely, constantly beginning and never bringing anything to an end.

Grant the reputation on every visible count — purity of doctrine, unity, uniformity in worship, decency and order, with no unhappy divisions on record — and locate the fault entirely in what does not fall under the observation of men: a form of godliness but not the power, and what little life remained ready to die. Draw the pastoral consequence from the titles, that to every minister and church a measure of the Spirit is given to improve, not ordinarily withdrawn until they forfeit it by misimprovement. Explain the works not found filled up as an emptiness inside the form: prayers not filled up with holy desires, alms-deeds not with true charity, sabbaths not with devotion of soul.

Read the address as a rebuke of one man, the angel being the bishop, who is not diligent in correcting the bad: to thyself thou seemest to be alive, but if thou art not watchful in the correction of the wicked thou wilt be numbered among the dead; and if a ruler has not striven to incite others, though he appear guiltless before men his works are not perfect before God. Or class the Sardians as men who are careless and carry on other transactions in the world than they ought, Christians only in name, since it is not enough for a tree to live and have no fruit, nor to confess Christ without having him in our work.

debates.question: What is the deadness at Sardis, and who is charged with it?

sides.position: A simple want of religion in the body — no prevailing error or false doctrine is named here, as it is at Ephesus and Thyatira
A reputation deserved on every visible count, with the fault entirely in what men cannot observe: a form of godliness without the power
The failure of one man — the angel is the bishop, not diligent in correcting the wicked, and numbered with the dead for it
The withdrawal of the Spirit, repeatedly grieved and about finally to depart

debates.question: Who is the call to remember addressed to?

sides.position: The Sardians themselves, recalled to the ardour with which they first embraced the gospel
The church since the Reformation, whose received and heard doctrines of grace are now almost buried in forgetfulness — this is exactly our case

outliers.note: Alone suspects a counterfeit of this scene, taking the devil's showing our Saviour all the kingdoms of the world from an exceeding high mountain as an attempt to mimic and out-do it, all in a moment of time where this was gradual.

Alone diagnoses the mechanism rather than the symptom, arguing that living with the credit of superior piety makes it easy to grow satisfied with the reputation, and that self-satisfaction is the road to self-deception.

Alone spends the whole of his note on the succession at Sardis, naming its pastors and bishops century by century from Melito in the second to the councils of the eighth, without touching the exposition at all.

themes: And unto the angel of the church in Sardis write; These things saith he that hath the seven Spirits of God, and the seven stars; I know thy works, that thou hast a name that thou livest, and art dead.
Be watchful, and strengthen the things which remain, that are ready to die: for I have not found thy works perfect before God.

Remember therefore how thou hast received and heard, and hold fast, and repent. If therefore thou shalt not watch, I will come on thee as a thief, and thou shalt not know what hour I will come upon thee.

4.pericope_label: A few names even in Sardis which have not defiled their garments

schools.summary: Guard the praise: the words cannot be understood of absolute purity, and what is commended is that in the deathlike self-complacent lethargy around them they had kept earnest in the pursuit of holiness. Distinguish two whites, the undefiled robe of the verse before and the lustrous white of glory promised here, and report a suggested reference to the dyes for which Sardis was celebrated; or take white simply as the emblem of innocence, the reward being that those who kept their garments uncontaminated on earth should appear so clothed in heaven. On the worthiness, deny any claim of merit and say only that there is a fitness in their appearing there, since they have the character to which God has promised eternal life — worthy in a relative sense, not in the sense in which God and Christ are called worthy. On the blotting out, either find a positive assurance of security, since no one can have access to that book but he who keeps it, or report the opposite reading, that a process of erasure is ever going on besides the process of entering, and when the soul has finally taken its choice for evil the pen is drawn through the guilty name.

Count the few a different way, not few in comparison of the world, in which sense all the elect are few, but few in comparison of the formal lifeless professors this church abounds with; for there may not only be hypocrites in churches but a majority of them.

Explain the idiom from church practice, members being enrolled in a book when admitted, so that names stand for the people who bore them; and the defiled garments from Jewish usage, in which holiness is the garb of the soul and evil actions stains upon it, citing a parable of a king who gave royal garments to his servants — the prudent folded them away, the foolish wore them at their daily labour, and when the king asked for them the clean were laid up in his wardrobe and those who brought them spotted went to prison. Supply the practice behind the blotting out as well: the great council stripped a faulty priest of his white garments and clothed him in black, and a citizen was struck from the register when his citizenship was forfeited. Alongside this, state plainly that the overcomer's name will not be blotted out like that of the angel of the church at Sardis, and that a few good among many bad are doubly acceptable to God.

Call the worthiness not a legal but a gospel worthiness, not merit but meetness. Hold the two sides of the blotting out together by dividing the enrolment: men may be enrolled in the registers of the church as baptized and professing, and such a name may be blotted out when it appears that it was but a name, such men being left of God to blot out their own names by gross and open wickedness; but the names of those that overcome shall never be blotted out.

Fasten on the wording, that he said not a few but a few names, for he calleth his own sheep by name and writes their names in heaven; and take the promise of white raiment as an invitation to all men to imitate those who have kept the robe of baptism undefiled.

debates.question: Does the promise not to blot out a name imply that names are blotted out?

sides.position: No — it is a positive assurance of security, since no one can have access to that book but he who keeps it
Yes — a process of erasure is ever going on besides the process of entering, and the pen is drawn through the guilty name
Yes, and a particular name is meant: the overcomer's will not be blotted out like that of the angel of the church at Sardis
Both, once the enrolment is divided: a name entered as baptized and professing may be blotted out, but the names of those that overcome never

debates.question: In what sense are the undefiled 'few'?

sides.position: Few in comparison of the formal lifeless professors, not of the world — there may be not only hypocrites in churches but a majority of them
Few and yet unseparated: they had not withdrawn from the rest, or the angel of Sardis would not have had them, and it was his fault that they were so few

outliers.note: Alone supplies the antiquarian practice behind both figures, the Jewish parable of the king's royal garments returned clean or spotted, and the stripping of a faulty priest's white garments with the striking of a citizen from the register.
Alone turns the commendation of the few back on the man addressed, observing that it was no virtue of his that they were unspotted and his fault that they were but few.
Alone presses the difference between a few and a few names, on the ground that he calleth his own sheep by name and writes their names in heaven.

themes: Thou hast a few names even in Sardis which have not defiled their garments; and they shall walk with me in white: for they are worthy.
He that overcometh, the same shall be clothed in white raiment; and I will not blot out his name out of the book of life, but I will confess his name before my Father, and before his angels.
He that hath an ear, let him hear what the Spirit saith unto the churches.

7.pericope_label: He that hath the key of David: behold, I have set before thee an open door

schools.summary: Derive the name from Attalus Philadelphus, king of Pergamos, place the town on the slopes of Mount Tmolus in a district whose soil favoured the vine, with the head of Bacchus on its coins; the region was volcanic and few cities suffered more from earthquakes, yet of all the seven it had the longest life as a Christian city, and the historian's judgment is that Philadelphia alone has been saved, a column in a scene of ruins. Add that it was rebuilt by Tiberius after the great earthquake and for a time called Neo-Caesarea, and that it has been called the Missionary City. Be exact on the titles: holy carries the idea of consecration, of what is set apart to God, and true expresses more than the opposite of false, being the reality in contrast with the shadow, the antitype with the type. On the key of David, record that some early commentators found in it the key of knowledge which the scribes had taken away, and answer that this is not wrong but too limited, only a corner of the meaning; the word David and the derivation from the prophet point wider, to Christ as the true Steward of the house of David, against whom the self-seeking stewards vainly claimed a right of exclusion from synagogue or church. But be careful the other way too, since applying the same terms to Peter and to Christ does not prove the steward in the prophet a type of Christ, but merely that the same words admit of different applications. On the open door, canvass the senses — ability to do good, access to the heavenly palace, escape from danger and persecution — reject the last, and take it either in the largest sense, that this church had no restraint upon it at all, or more narrowly as an opportunity for missionary effort in spite of the Jewish hostility; the reward of a little strength is a door opened. On the synagogue, deny that conversion is necessarily meant, or read the promise as covering only some of them and expect the suspected to be transformed by time into the respected.

Say that holiness essentially dwells in him and from him all holiness is derived, and that he is the fountain of truth, who can neither lie nor be imposed on. Press the sovereignty in the key: David could open or shut the kingdom of Israel to whom he pleased and was not bound to leave it even to his eldest son, and as applied here the words show Christ absolute. Read the little strength as little political authority or influence, and expect the adversaries to be obliged to sue to the Christians for toleration in the most abject manner.

Take the name for the church's character, from the brotherly love for which the citizens were eminent as a civil fraternity, and observe that no fault is found with this church, though doubtless there were faults in it of common infirmity, for love covers such faults. Itemise the acts of Christ's government: he opens a door of opportunity to his churches, of utterance to his ministers, of entrance by opening the heart; and shuts heaven against the foolish virgins who have slept away their day of grace. Hear a gentle reproof in the little strength, that a little grace is not proportioned to so wide a door, and though Christ accepts a little strength believers should not rest satisfied in a little. On the synagogue, hold that they shall be convinced they were in the wrong and desire to be taken into communion.

debates.question: What is the opened door set before Philadelphia?

sides.position: Access rather than escape, and in the largest sense — this church had no restraint upon it at all
More narrowly, a good opportunity for missionary effort in spite of the Jewish hostility
The liberty and opportunity Christ himself has kept open against many adversaries, which no man can shut unless we provoke him to shut it

debates.question: What does it mean that the synagogue shall come and worship before their feet?

sides.position: Not necessarily conversion — enemies constrained to render respect and acknowledge that the church enjoys God's favour
Conviction and communion — they shall know they were in the wrong and desire to be admitted
Political submission — the adversaries obliged to sue to the Christians for toleration and protection in the most abject manner

outliers.note: Alone takes the key of David beyond the key of knowledge to the stewardship of Isaiah's prophecy, making Christ the true Steward against whom the self-seeking stewards of synagogue and church vainly claimed a right of exclusion.
Alone reads the city's name as the church's character, tracing the brotherly love of a civil fraternity into the one church in which no fault is found, on the ground that love covers such faults.

Alone guards against over-reading the Old Testament source, quoting the caution that applying the same terms to Peter and to Christ does not prove Isaiah's steward a type of Christ, but only that the same words admit of different applications.

themes: And to the angel of the church in Philadelphia write; These things saith he that is holy, he that is true, he that hath the key of David, he that openeth, and no man shutteth; and shutteth, and no man openeth;
I know thy works: behold, I have set before thee an open door, and no man can shut it: for thou hast a little strength, and hast kept my word, and hast not denied my name.
Behold, I will make them of the synagogue of Satan, which say they are Jews, and are not, but do lie; behold, I will make them to come and worship before thy feet, and to know that I have loved thee.

10.pericope_label: Him that overcometh will I make a pillar in the temple of my God

schools.summary: State the principle first, that the one who keeps God's word is kept, and then narrow the promise: it does not mean being kept away from the tribulation but being kept out from it, the head held above the waters. Or narrow it further, holding that they would not be kept from calamity at all but from the temptation of apostasy in calamity, since one of the highest rewards of patience in one trial is the grace to bear another, God not leaving those who have shown that they will not leave him. Refuse to identify the hour, noting that nothing can be determined with certainty, though the earthquake recorded by a Roman historian, which sank twelve cities of Asia Minor in a single night and deeply affected Philadelphia, may be mentioned. On the pillar, observe that Philadelphia was a city of earthquakes, so that an unshaken pillar was a pointed image, and that inscriptions may still be found on the sides of the marble pillars surviving among its ruins; take it that those who overcome will prove real supports to the great Christian temple, or keep both senses, calling the metaphor doubly significant of being firmly fixed and of giving stability to the building, and find in the going out no more that fixity of character is at last achieved.

Take the Gospel to be called the word of his patience because it gives an account of the patience of Christ in the midst of all his outward meanness and humiliation, and because it is the means of implanting and increasing that grace in those who receive it. Put the hour of temptation in the future altogether, as a trial to come upon the reformed churches at the beginning of this period, out of which the truly godly will be delivered, antichrist destroyed, and the latter day glory brought in.

Read the promise as plain exemption, that they should not enter into the temptation at all but it should pass over them. Name the hour: it is the persecution under Trajan, and it deserved the name of temptation rather than mere affliction because the two preceding persecutions were under the monsters Nero and Domitian, whereas Trajan was so admired for his goodness, and his persecution of such a nature, that it did thoroughly try them that dwelt on the earth. Read the whole promise of the pillar through the sanctuary: the two pillars of the temple at Jerusalem were stability and strength, and to have the name written is to be made a priest, since the priest wore Holiness to the Lord upon his forehead, while the names of the twelve tribes on the high priest's breastplate give place to the apostles of the new Jerusalem.

Make the same threefold point about the word of patience — that the gospel is the fruit of God's patience to a sinful world, sets before men the exemplary patience of Christ, and calls those who receive it to patience — and add the sequence it implies: a day of gospel peace is a day of God's patience, seldom so well improved as it should be, and therefore often followed by an hour of trial. Decline to date the hour and state a rule instead, that when the trial is general and universal it is usually the shorter. On the pillar, deny that the overcomer supports anything, since heaven needs no such props, and make him a monument instead — one that shall never be defaced nor removed, as many stately pillars erected in honour of Roman emperors and generals have been.

debates.question: What is the hour of temptation that shall come upon all the world?

sides.position: The persecution under Trajan, a temptation rather than a mere affliction because the emperor was so admired for his goodness
Undeterminable — though the earthquake that sank twelve cities of Asia Minor in one night may be what is meant
Still future: a trial upon the reformed churches, ending in the destruction of antichrist and the latter day glory

debates.question: Does 'I will keep thee from the hour' promise exemption or preservation?

sides.position: Exemption — they should not enter into the temptation at all, but it should pass over them
Preservation through it — not kept away from the tribulation but kept out from it, the head held above the waters
Preservation of a narrower kind — not kept from calamity at all, but from the temptation of apostasy in calamity

debates.question: Does the overcomer, as a pillar, support the temple?

sides.position: Yes — those who overcome will prove real supports to the great Christian temple
No — heaven needs no such props; the pillar is a monument that shall never be defaced nor removed
Both senses at once — the metaphor is doubly significant of being firmly fixed and of giving stability to the building

outliers.note: Alone points to the marble pillars still standing among the ruins of Philadelphia, with inscriptions on their sides, as the local image behind the promise of a pillar written upon.

Alone reads the promise through the sanctuary, taking the two pillars of the temple for stability and strength and the writing of the name as ordination to priesthood, since the priest wore Holiness to the Lord upon his forehead.

Alone explains why the persecution under Trajan counted as a temptation rather than an affliction, since the two before it were under the monsters Nero and Domitian, while Trajan was admired for his goodness.

themes: Because thou hast kept the word of my patience, I also will keep thee from the hour of temptation, which shall come upon all the world, to try them that dwell upon the earth.
Behold, I come quickly: hold that fast which thou hast, that no man take thy crown.

Him that overcometh will I make a pillar in the temple of my God, and he shall go no more out: and I will write upon him the name of my God, and the name of the city of my God, which is new Jerusalem, which cometh down out of heaven from my God: and I will write upon him my new name.
He that hath an ear, let him hear what the Spirit saith unto the churches.

14.pericope_label: Because thou art lukewarm, I will spue thee out of my mouth

schools.summary: Name the city from Laodice, wife of the second Antiochus, note that it shared with Thyatira and Sardis in the dye trade, its wools famous for the rich blackness of their colour, and report the fact that tells most: when the city suffered in the great earthquake its people rebuilt without applying to the Imperial Treasury, as the neighbouring towns were compelled to do. Add the banking and the manufacture of woollen carpets, the worship of Asklepios with its medical school, and the name the City of Compromise, observing that no praise at all is bestowed on this church. On the titles, observe that the Amen is used here alone as a personal name, the Hebrew word for verily, chosen to recall how often our Lord prefaced his own utterances with it; and that the beginning must be taken actively, not first among the created but the origination of all creation, the point needed in a church tempted to worship inferior principalities, and the answer to the Arians. On the threat, note that tepid water tends to sicken and provoke a vomit, the word chosen meaning rejection with extreme disgust.

Describe the temper that earns the threat: a lukewarm professor serves God and mammon, halts between two opinions, cares little which religion is best, yet keeps up a round of duty and rests in the external form, unconcerned about the life and power of godliness.

Say that by these titles he prepares them for the humiliating truths he is about to declare. Reach the preference for cold by another road, calling them neither heathens nor Christians, too good for hell and too bad for heaven, and quoting both a couplet on being to good and evil equally bent, at once a devil and a saint, and the pagan moralist's rule that a man ought to be one kind of man, either good or bad. Then draw a doctrine from the wish rather than a rebuke: it plainly implies that our Lord does not work on us irresistibly, as fire does on the water it heats. And keep the door open, adding that the rejection stands unless thou repent.

Describe a wall of vast compass, three marble theatres and a city built like Rome upon seven hills, and end where the others do not, with the ruins that lie there still as an awful monument of the wrath of the Lamb — and yet this was one of the seven golden candlesticks, for a corrupt church is still a church. State the principle flatly: if religion is worth anything it is worth everything, there is no room for neutrality, and an open enemy shall have fairer quarter than a perfidious neuter. Name the disguises lukewarmness wears, since men call it charity, meekness, moderation and largeness of soul; it is nauseous to Christ, and makes those so who allow themselves in it.

debates.question: Why would Christ rather have them cold than lukewarm?

sides.position: For three reasons: such a state is more honest, more honourable, and more hopeful — Saul of Tarsus always had the elements of greatness, Judas never did, and the most hopeless condition is to enter the church deceived
Because a man ought to be decided and of one kind — these were neither heathens nor Christians, too good for hell and too bad for heaven
Because there is no room for neutrality: if religion is worth anything it is worth everything, and an open enemy shall have fairer quarter than a perfidious neuter

debates.question: What follows from Christ's wishing them cold or hot?

sides.position: A rebuke: their state is the worst temper in the world and nauseous to him
A doctrine: the wish plainly implies that he does not work on us irresistibly, as fire does on the water it heats

outliers.note: Alone sets Saul of Tarsus against Judas Iscariot to show why open opposition is a more hopeful character than lukewarm profession, the one always carrying the elements of greatness and the other, even under the Redeemer's teaching, never.

Alone brings in outside verse and pagan philosophy on the same point, quoting a couplet on being to good and evil equally bent and a moralist's rule that a man ought to be one kind of man, either good or bad.

Alone ends the description of the city with its ruins as an awful monument of the wrath of the Lamb, while insisting that this was nonetheless one of the seven golden candlesticks, for a corrupt church is still a church.

themes: And unto the angel of the church of the Laodiceans write; These things saith the Amen, the faithful and true witness, the beginning of the creation of God;
I know thy works, that thou art neither cold nor hot: I would thou wert cold or hot.
So then because thou art lukewarm, and neither cold nor hot, I will spue thee out of my mouth.

17.pericope_label: Thou sayest, I am rich; buy of me gold tried in the fire

schools.summary: Observe that the church carried the pride of a wealthy city into its spiritual life, so that it was rich in pride and conceit but poor in grace and ignorant of its poverty — the reverse of Smyrna, poor in wealth and rich in grace. Take the five words as an amplification of the reason for the rejection, calling this church the type and embodiment of wretchedness: their wealth led them into a quiet and unaggressive kind of religion, and self-complacency taught them to believe the best of themselves and then to believe in themselves. They were hypocrites who did not know they were hypocrites, and on that quote the argument that the victim of passion may be converted, and the gay and the thoughtless and the ambitious, but that nobody can convert the hypocrite, who cannot know he is one by the very law of his character, and the greater hypocrite he is the more sincere he must think himself. Identify the counsel with the city's own trades: the eye-salve is a famous Phrygian powder made at Laodicea, the gold answers to its banking and the white raiment to the black wools it sold. Hear irony in the invitation, since how could the poor and naked buy, but find the sting drawn by the prophet's invitation to buy without money and without price. Argue that the gold stands for love rather than faith, since the Laodiceans were like those who had gifts and tongues and understanding and liberality but lacked the fervent love without which all is nothing, and love is the only coin which passes at heaven's mart; or make it religion at large, as the most precious of the metals stands for the most precious of possessions. Be precise about the two verbs of the rebuke: the first is the word used of the work of the Spirit and signifies to bring conviction rather than empty censure, the second signifies to educate by means of correction; and the pronoun is emphatic, calling attention to the fidelity of Christ's love against the weak partiality of human love. Note too that the zeal commanded is the very word for boiling, set deliberately against their lukewarmness.

Read the wealth as partly literal, since riches seldom do the churches of Christ any good, and did none in the time of Constantine; and partly spiritual, since she was rich not in grace but in external gifts and in good works, on which she too much trusted for salvation. Set out at length what Christ is as a Counsellor, and that the substance of his counsel is to come to him for grace, life and salvation, for pardon, peace and righteousness.

Identify the particular error behind the confidence, that they rested in what they had already received and seemed to think that once in grace must be still in grace. Press the first word hard, since the term rendered wretched is used of men worn out with grievous labour, as those in a stone quarry or condemned to the mines, so that instead of being heirs of the kingdom they were in the condition of the most abject slaves. Take the gold for faith that shall stand in every trial, purified in the furnace of affliction, the white raiment for holiness of heart and life, and the eyesalve for the enlightening influences of the Spirit. Then make the application personal and startled: whomsoever I love — even thee, thou poor Laodicean; O how much has his unwearied love to do.

debates.question: What does the gold tried in the fire stand for?

sides.position: Faith — faith that shall stand in every trial, purified in the furnace of affliction
Love — the grace this church lacked, and the only coin which passes at heaven's mart
Religion at large, gold being the most precious of the metals and so an emblem of the most precious of possessions

debates.question: What made this church incapable of seeing its own state?

sides.position: Hypocrisy that does not know itself — the hypocrite cannot know he is one by the very law of his character, and the greater he is the more sincere he thinks himself
Resting in what had already been received, on the assumption that once in grace must be still in grace
Mistaking the furniture of religion for the thing: learning taken for religion, gifts for grace, wit for wisdom, ordinances for the God of ordinances

outliers.note: Alone identifies the eye-salve as a famous Phrygian powder for the eyes manufactured at Laodicea itself, which ties the whole counsel to the three trades of the city.

Alone works the lexicon of the word rendered wretched, which is used of men worn out with grievous labour, as those in a stone quarry or condemned to the mines, so that the supposed heirs of the kingdom are described as the most abject slaves.

Alone turns aside from the rebuke to set out at length what Christ is as a Counsellor, and reads the church's wealth partly as the literal riches which did the churches no good in the time of Constantine.

themes: Because thou sayest, I am rich, and increased with goods, and have need of nothing; and knowest not that thou art wretched, and miserable, and poor, and blind, and naked:

I counsel thee to buy of me gold tried in the fire, that thou mayest be rich; and white raiment, that thou mayest be clothed, and that the shame of thy nakedness do not appear; and anoint thine eyes with eyesalve, that thou mayest see.
As many as I love, I rebuke and chasten: be zealous therefore, and repent.

20.pericope_label: Behold, I stand at the door, and knock

schools.summary: Draw two things from the act of knocking: that he desires admittance, and that he recognises the right of the man within to open or not. He does not obtrude himself, nor employ force; if admitted he comes in and dwells, if rejected he turns quietly away, perhaps to knock again, perhaps never to come back. From the same image take the decisive point, that the attempt at reconciliation begins with the Saviour, who presents himself at the door as if he desired the friendship of man, salvation being never represented in the Scriptures as originated by man. Keep both readings of the scene, calling it a picture of the Lord's advent which is true also of the individual response to his call, and call the supper fellowship in the Messianic kingdom, purely metaphorical. On the throne, find two mentioned: Christ's own, which glorified saints are promised a share in, and the Father's, which is the power of divine majesty, wherein none may sit but God and the God-man; and read the promise as the last step of a series carrying the thought from the garden through the wilderness and the temple to the throne. Notice where this promise falls, with an eye to the despondency that follows the collapse of self-satisfied imaginations: though their religion has been proved an empty thing, the highest place is within reach of the lowest, and the faintest spark of grace may be fanned into the mightiest flame. Then look back over all seven, noting that each message begins and ends alike, each is suited to the actual condition of its church, and the Shepherd lays bare the particular peril in each.

Read the standing at the door as the near approach of Christ to judgment and the knocking as the notice given by the forerunners of his coming, observed by few, so general a sleepiness having seized all professors, and issuing in the midnight cry.

Put the emphasis on the handle: the opening must be the sinner's own act, done with power received from his offended Lord, who will make no forcible entry. Support it from two rabbinic sayings, one in which God asks his children to open him a door of repentance no wider than a needle's eye and promises to open doors through which cattle may pass, another in which the doors stay shut against the man who conceals his sin before the holy King but fly open to him who confesses it. Divide the promise of the supper in two, that to sup with him is to hold communion and feed him with the bread of life, and that he shall sup with Christ when brought at last to everlasting glory. Do not divide the thrones but press their identity, since Christ has conquered and is set down upon the Father's throne, and it is on that same throne that those faithful unto death are finally to sit — how astonishing this state of exaltation, and who can conceive its dignity. Observe that this is the worst of the seven churches and yet the most eminent of the promises are made to it, which shows that the worst may repent, finally conquer, and attain the highest state of glory. Close by noting the arrangement, that the call to hear stands before the promise in the first three letters and after it in the last four, dividing the seven in two; and that the victory to which these promises are annexed is not the ordinary victory of every believer but a special victory over great and peculiar temptations, won by those strong in faith.

debates.question: Is the knocking at the door an appeal to the individual heart or a sign of the advent?

sides.position: The advent — the near approach of Christ to judgment, its notice given by forerunners and signs, issuing in the midnight cry
The individual heart — and the act proves that reconciliation begins with the Saviour, who will not force the door
Both — a picture of the Lord's advent which is true also of the individual response to his call

debates.question: Is the throne the overcomer is promised the same throne as the Father's?

sides.position: No — two thrones are mentioned, and in the Father's, which is the power of divine majesty, none may sit but God and the God-man
Yes — Christ's throne and the Father's are the same, and it is on that same throne that those faithful unto death are finally to sit

outliers.note: Alone brings rabbinic sayings to the door, one promising that a repentance opened no wider than a needle's eye will be answered with doors wide enough for cattle, another that the doors stay shut against the man who conceals his sin and fly open to him who confesses it.

Alone analyses the act of knocking itself into a claim and a concession, that the knocker desires admittance and yet recognises the householder's right to refuse, so that he turns quietly away if rejected.
Alone reads the last promise as the summit of an ascending series running through the whole seven, from the garden of Eden through the wilderness and the temple to the throne.

themes: Behold, I stand at the door, and knock: if any man hear my voice, and open the door, I will come in to him, and will sup with him, and he with me.
To him that overcometh will I grant to sit with me in my throne, even as I also overcame, and am set down with my Father in his throne.
He that hath an ear, let him hear what the Spirit saith unto the churches.
